questions.subtopic: 2.15 The solution set of 2^x >= x^2, where the two exact intersections x = 2 and x = 4 are the only ones a natural window shows and the third intersection is at a negative value of x that the window excludes

figure.caption: The graphs of y = 2^x and y = x^2 on 0 <= x <= 5, showing the two intersections this window contains.

questions.challenge_mechanism: The two intersections that a natural window shows are both exact, at x = 2 and x = 4, and that exactness is what makes the window look complete. The inequality has a third solution at x = -0.7667, on the other side of the y-axis, where the exponential curve has flattened towards zero and the parabola has not. A candidate who reads the diagram and reports the two visible intersections has answered a question about the interval 0 <= x <= 5 rather than about the real numbers. The lever is a single one: the domain the search is carried out on, not the algebra of the inequality, decides the answer.
questions.question:
The diagram shows the graphs of $y = 2^{x}$ and $y = x^{2}$ drawn on the interval $0 \le x \le 5$, together with the two points at which the curves meet inside that interval. The inequality
$$2^{x} \ge x^{2}$$
is to be solved for all real values of $x$. The interval on which the diagram is drawn is not the whole of the real line, and the diagram says nothing about any part of the line that lies outside it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the diagram, determine the set of values of $x$ with $0 \le x \le 5$ for which $2^{x} \ge x^{2}$, and state how many intersections of the two curves the diagram shows.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the diagram alone cannot establish the complete solution set of the inequality over the real numbers, and state what the behaviour of the two curves on the negative side of the $y$-axis shows that the diagram leaves out.

parts.label: c
parts.text: By a numerical method, determine the negative value of $x$ at which $2^{x} = x^{2}$, giving your answer correct to four decimal places, and show that this is the only negative solution.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Hence solve $2^{x} \ge x^{2}$ for all real $x$, and justify why there is no further intersection beyond the largest one you have already used.

questions.answer:
**(a)** The diagram is drawn on $0 \le x \le 5$ and shows the two curves meeting at $(2,\,4)$ and $(4,\,16)$, since $2^{2} = 4 = 2^{2}$ and $2^{4} = 16 = 4^{2}$ (A1). Reading the sign of the difference between the curves off the diagram, the solid exponential curve lies above the dashed parabola from $x = 0$ up to $x = 2$, the parabola lies above the exponential curve between the two crossings, and the exponential curve is again above from $x = 4$ onwards (M1). For example at $x = 1$ the values are $2$ and $1$, at $x = 3$ they are $8$ and $9$, and at $x = 5$ they are $32$ and $25$ (A1). So on this interval the inequality holds for
$$0 \le x \le 2 \quad\text{and}\quad 4 \le x \le 5,$$
and the diagram shows exactly two intersections.
**(b)** The diagram begins at $x = 0$, so it cannot say anything about the curve for $x < 0$. On the negative side the two curves behave in opposite ways: $y = 2^{x}$ falls towards zero as $x$ becomes more negative, while $y = x^{2}$ grows without bound (M1). Immediately to the left of the origin the exponential curve is still the larger of the two, because $2^{0} = 1 > 0 = 0^{2}$, but far to the left the parabola is much the larger, because $2^{-10} = 0.00098$ against $100$ (A1). A curve that starts above the other and finishes below it must cross it at least once in between, so there is at least one intersection with a negative $x$-coordinate, and the diagram is drawn on an interval that excludes it (A1). The complete solution set therefore cannot be read off the diagram.
**(c)** Define $f(x) = 2^{x} - x^{2}$ for $x < 0$. At $x = -1$,
$$f(-1) = 2^{-1} - 1 = -0.5 < 0,$$
while at $x = -0.5$,
$$f(-0.5) = 2^{-0.5} - 0.25 = 0.70711 - 0.25 = +0.45711 > 0,$$
so a root lies between $-1$ and $-0.5$ (M1). Repeated bisection, or a numerical solver, narrows that bracket to
$$x = -0.7666646960\ldots \qquad\text{so}\qquad x \approx -0.7667 \;(A1),$$
correct to four decimal places. To see that there is only one negative root, differentiate:
$$f'(x) = 2^{x}\ln 2 - 2x .$$
For $x < 0$ the first term is positive because $2^{x} > 0$ and $\ln 2 > 0$, and the second term $-2x$ is positive as well. Hence $f'(x) > 0$ for every $x < 0$, so $f$ is strictly increasing on the whole negative half-line and can change sign there exactly once (A1). Since $f(x) \to -\infty$ as $x \to -\infty$ while $f(0) = 1 > 0$, that one sign change does occur, and the root is unique.
**(d)** Combining the three intervals, $2^{x} \ge x^{2}$ exactly when
$$-0.7667 \le x \le 2 \quad\text{or}\quad x \ge 4 \;(A1).$$
It remains to show that there is no intersection beyond $x = 4$. Consider the ratio $g(x) = \dfrac{2^{x}}{x^{2}}$ for $x \ge 5$. Differentiating,
$$g'(x) = \frac{2^{x}\,(x\ln 2 - 2)}{x^{3}},$$
and for $x \ge 5$ the factor $x\ln 2 - 2$ is at least $5(0.69315) - 2 = 1.4657 > 0$, so $g$ is strictly increasing on $x \ge 5$ (M1). At $x = 5$ the ratio is $32/25 = 1.28 > 1$, so $g(x) > 1$ for every $x \ge 5$, which means $2^{x} > x^{2}$ throughout (A1). The curves therefore do not meet again, and the largest intersection is the one at $x = 4$ (A1). The complete solution set is
$$\{x \in \mathbb{R} : -0.7667 \le x \le 2\} \cup \{x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ge 4\},$$
with $-0.7667$ given to four decimal places.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) (A1) for the two intersection points $(2,\,4)$ and $(4,\,16)$ read from the diagram, (M1) for comparing the two curves between and outside the crossings, (A1) for the answer $0 \le x \le 2$ together with $4 \le x \le 5$. A candidate who states only the two points without giving the intervals scores (A1) and nothing more, because the question asks for the set of values of $x$ and not for the intersections. Accept $4 \le x$ written without the upper limit of $5$ provided the candidate has made clear that the diagram only extends to $x = 5$.
(b) (M1) for the observation that the diagram begins at $x = 0$ and therefore cannot rule out anything to the left of the $y$-axis, (A1) for the correct behaviour of the two curves as $x \to -\infty$, namely $2^{x} \to 0$ and $x^{2} \to +\infty$, (A1) for the intermediate value argument that the two must therefore cross on the negative side. An answer that merely says 'the graph is not wide enough' without naming the behaviour of either curve scores (M1) only. Do not accept 'the diagram is inaccurate' or 'the scale is too small' as a substitute: the diagram is accurate on the interval it covers, and the defect is the interval, not the drawing.
(c) (M1) for a correct bracket containing the negative root, for example by evaluating $f$ at $-1$ and at $-0.5$ and observing the sign change, (A1) for $-0.7667$ to four decimal places. Accept $-0.7666$ or $-0.76666$ as intermediate working but the final answer must be rounded to four decimal places; condone $-0.7667$ obtained from any valid numerical method, including a graph plotter or a Newton iteration. (A1) for the uniqueness argument, which requires the derivative and the observation that both of its terms are positive for $x < 0$. A candidate who asserts uniqueness because 'the graphs cross only once' has used the conclusion it is meant to prove and scores no mark for it.
(d) (A1) for the correct solution set, with both the closed interval and the half-line, (M1) for a valid argument that no intersection lies beyond $x = 4$, (A1) for completing that argument, and (A1) for the statement of the set in set notation. The ratio argument is not the only acceptable one: a candidate may instead show that $2^{x} > x^{2}$ at $x = 5$ and that the difference is increasing thereafter, or may argue from the exponential eventually dominating any polynomial. Any of these earns the two marks. Follow-through: a candidate whose negative root from (c) is wrong but whose set is written consistently with it keeps the marks in (d). Forfeits: answering $0 \le x \le 2$ or $x \ge 4$, which discards the negative interval; answering $-0.7667 \le x \le 2$ only, which discards the half-line; and writing $x \ge 4$ as $4 < x$, which loses the endpoint.
questions.explanation:
This item is about the difference between a window and a domain. The algebra needed is almost nothing: one substitution at $x = 2$, one at $x = 4$, a sign check at a few points, and a numerical root. What it tests is whether the candidate treats the diagram as evidence about the interval it covers or as evidence about the real line.

The reason the trap works is that both visible intersections are exact. At $x = 2$ the two sides are $4$ and $4$; at $x = 4$ they are $16$ and $16$. Exact answers feel like complete answers, and an inequality whose solution set is built from two integers is the shape a student expects. The third intersection is not merely outside the window, it is irrational, and it cannot be found by inspection at all. A candidate who has solved the equation $2^{x} = x^{2}$ by trying small integers has solved a different problem from the one asked.

The negative side is where the two curves separate in character. For $x < 0$ the exponential is a decreasing curve squeezed against the $x$-axis, while the parabola is an increasing one that will eventually be as large as anything. One starts above the other at the origin and ends below it, so a crossing is forced. That is the whole of part (b), and it is an argument about limits rather than about arithmetic: the candidate has to know where each curve goes, not what it equals at any particular point.

Uniqueness is the part that is easiest to assert and hardest to justify, so it is worth separating the two cases. On the negative half-line the derivative $2^{x}\ln 2 - 2x$ has both terms positive, which is unusually clean and settles the question with one line. On the far positive side that argument fails, because $-2x$ is negative there, and a different argument is needed: the ratio $2^{x}/x^{2}$ is increasing once $x\ln 2 > 2$, and it is already above $1$ at $x = 5$, so it never comes back down. Two different arguments for two different intervals is the honest structure of the problem, and a candidate who uses one argument twice will have asserted something false in one of the two places.

The figure is the natural window, drawn honestly, and that is exactly why it is not enough. It is not a misleading diagram; it is a correct diagram of the wrong interval. Recognising that a correct picture can still be an incomplete one is the single idea in this item, and it is why the item is claimed at difficulty 3: once the candidate has seen that the window is the lever, nothing else here is hard.

provenance.inspired_by: China gaokao exponential against polynomial: counting intersections and solving the resulting inequality on the real line
provenance.adaptation: The source genre asks how many times an exponential curve meets a polynomial curve, and answers it with a derivative or a parameter discussion. Here the derivative is not the lever: the item hands the candidate the two exact intersections and then asks what the picture they came from cannot show. The negative root is present in the source material as a numerical footnote; in this item it is the answer, and the two exact intersections are the decoy.

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Read the two intersections off the diagram, check that x = 2 and x = 4 both work exactly, notice that the two exact answers agree with the picture, and report the solution set as the two intervals the picture supports.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: Solving the equation by inspection is a technique that works here and proves nothing: the two exact roots are the only roots of the equation that are exact, and the third root is irrational and negative, so the inspection method returns a complete-looking answer that is missing one of the three intervals.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: The solution set is reported as 0 <= x <= 2 together with x >= 4, so every value of x between -0.7667 and 0 is wrongly excluded, and the item is answered as though the domain were the closed interval 0 <= x <= 5 that the diagram happens to be drawn on.

verification.method: A scan of f(x) = 2^x - x^2 over the range -6 <= x <= 20 at a step of 0.001, with every sign change bracketed and then bisected to 200 iterations, returns exactly three real roots: -0.7666646960, 2 and 4. The sign of the difference was checked at -2, -1, -0.9, -0.7, -0.5, 0, 1, 1.9, 2.1, 3, 3.9, 4.1, 5 and 10, and matches the three intervals asserted. The uniqueness argument on the negative side was checked by evaluating f'(x) = 2^x ln 2 - 2x at a grid of negative values, where it is positive everywhere, and the far-positive argument by checking that g(x) = 2^x / x^2 is increasing and greater than 1 at x = 5. Every value quoted in the answer was evaluated directly.
solution_skeleton: read the two intersections the diagram shows and the sign of the difference between them
explain why a diagram drawn from x = 0 cannot exclude an intersection at negative x
bracket the negative root by evaluating the difference at minus one and at minus a half
solve for the negative root numerically and round it to four decimal places
prove the negative root is unique by showing the difference is increasing there
show the exponential exceeds the parabola for all x at least five by a ratio argument
